deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler wants to produce provably prime numbers larger than a million without trial division of each candidate. His candidates are N = a²+1 (and (a²+1)/2 when a is odd). On this page he states and uses the following facts:
(i) Every divisor of a²+1 is a sum of two squares. He proved this in the 1750s, after Fermat, whose proof he regards as lost.
(ii) Every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two squares, and no prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) is.
(iii) Hence the only prime divisors of a²+1 are 2 and primes ≡ 1 (mod 4). No number ≡ 3 (mod 4) can divide a²+1, since such a number has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4).
(iv) Sieve. For each prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4) (5, 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, …), determine all a with P | a²+1. These a form two residue classes ±a₀ (mod P). Striking out every a in these classes leaves exactly the a for which a²+1 is prime; for odd a the same applies to (a²+1)/2. The factor 2 is handled separately: a odd gives 2 | a²+1.
(v) This motivates Problem 1: given a prime P = 4n+1, find all a with a² ≡ −1 (mod P). The next page solves it. Write P = p²+q² and use Euler's lemma that a divisor of a²+b² which is a sum of two squares gives a = pr+qs, b = ps−qr. Setting b = 1 forces ps−qr = ±1, so r/s is the continued-fraction neighbour of p/q. Then a ≡ ±(pr+qs) (mod P). Equivalently a ≡ ±p·q⁻¹ (mod P), computed by the Euclidean algorithm.
In modern terms this is a sieve of Eratosthenes adapted to the polynomial x²+1, i.e. a sieve over the roots of x² ≡ −1 mod p. It serves the search for large primes and bears on Landau's problem of whether infinitely many n²+1 are prime.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The sieve is complete provided every prime P up to about a_max is used: if a²+1 ≤ a_max²+1 is composite, it has a prime factor ≤ a_max. This bound is not spelled out here, but it is implicit.
The phrase 'Fermat's proof is to be regarded as lost' is a historical judgment; no proof by Fermat is extant.

ideas.what: Prime divisors of a²+1 are 2 or ≡1 mod 4; every divisor of a²+1 is a sum of two squares
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic character of −1 / divisors of the binary form x²+y²
ideas.where_published: Euler E228 (De numeris qui sunt aggregata duorum quadratorum) and E241 (Demonstratio theorematis Fermatiani omnem numerum primum formae 4n+1 esse summam duorum quadratorum)

ideas.what: Sieving the values a²+1 by the residue classes a ≡ ±√−1 mod p, for primes p ≡ 1 mod 4, to list the primes of the form a²+1 and (a²+1)/2
ideas.modern_name: Polynomial sieve of Eratosthenes (sieve over roots of a polynomial mod p)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, in this paper E283; widely cited in discussions of Landau's fourth problem
ideas.where_published: E283 itself (Novi Commentarii 9, 1762/3, publ. 1764); discussed in Sandifer's 'How Euler Did It' columns and in Lemmermeyer's historical notes

ideas.what: Problem 1: find all solutions of a² ≡ −1 mod P from the representation P = p²+q²
ideas.modern_name: Square root of −1 mod p via p/q (inverse of the Hermite–Serret/Cornacchia construction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (here); the reverse direction is credited to Hermite–Serret (1848) and Cornacchia (1908)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known exposition of Euler's sieve for primes of the form a²+1. The underlying facts are his own published theorems on sums of two squares, and the method is already documented in the historical literature. Nothing on the page appears to be unrecorded.
